turns.prompt_text: Who is Lord the lady? The musician who was a pop star for a little while in the 2010s. She even had a South Park episode on her
turns.response_html:
You're thinking of Lorde, whose real name is Ella Marija Lani Yelich-O'Connor. She is a Grammy-winning New Zealand singer-songwriter who gained massive global fame in 2013 with her hit song "Royals".

The South Park connection is one of the show's most famous running gags. In Season 18, it is revealed that Randy Marsh (Stan's dad) is secretly the real Lorde.

The joke started when South Park creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker originally had Randy pretend to be Lorde just for a quick gag to perform at a party. When a journalist criticized the show for supposedly mocking Lorde's appearance, the creators leaned into it entirely — dedicating the rest of the season to the premise that the 45-year-old male geologist was actually the 17-year-old female pop star, producing his hit tracks in the men's bathroom using a recording app and Auto-Tune.

The show even released a full original song by Randy as Lorde called "Push (Feeling Good on a Wednesday)". The secret vocals for that track were actually provided by another massive pop star, Sia.

The real Lorde thought the parody was hilarious and even sang a rendition of Randy's "I am Lorde, ya ya ya" catchphrase during a subsequent interview.

When "Royals" came out in 2013, mainstream pop was dominated by flashy, high-energy club anthems that glorified wealth, partying, and excess—artists like Kesha, Katy Perry, and early Lady Gaga.

Lorde offered a stark contrast in both sound and subject matter, which is why "Royals" hit so hard.

The Themes of "Royals" and Early Lorde

Her lyrics focused on authentic teenage reality rather than fantasy. She wrote about suburban boredom, anxiety, growing up, and the gap between normal life and what was on TV.

"Royals" specifically became a cultural phenomenon because it functioned as a class-conscious critique of pop materialism. In the song, she explicitly calls out the tropes of pop and hip-hop (diamonds, Maybachs, "Cristal, Maybach, diamonds on your timepiece") and declares that "that kind of luxe just ain't for us".

She wasn't singing from the perspective of an aspirational pop star; she was singing from the perspective of a 16-year-old kid from New Zealand looking at American pop culture and finding it deeply unrelatable.

Why "Royals" Caught On

  • Relatability: Following the 2008 financial crisis, millennials and Gen Z were facing a bleak economic reality. A song that explicitly rejected unattainable wealth resonated with a generation that knew they wouldn't have it.
  • Sonic Minimalism: Compared to the over-produced, synth-heavy EDM-pop of 2013, "Royals" was shockingly bare. It relied on snapping, a simple beat, and her layered vocals. This "lo-fi" sound made her stand out immediately on the radio.
  • The "Alt-Pop" Shift: "Royals" essentially cleared the path for the moody, minimalist "alt-pop" that would define the rest of the decade. Without Lorde proving that dark, introspective pop could be commercially viable, artists like Billie Eilish, Halsey, and Olivia Rodrigo might not have had the same mainstream runway.

While "Royals" did face some criticism—with some writers arguing that by singling out tropes like gold teeth and Cristal, she was specifically critiquing Black culture and hip-hop—the prevailing legacy of the song is its anti-imperialist, anti-materialist stance. She essentially popped the bubble of 2010s party anthems, and pop music shifted to match her tone.

turns.prompt_text: How long had she been writing songs before that? Did she have an upgrading of musical talent? What drove her to create these songs?
turns.response_html:
⚖️She had actually been writing for a few years before "Royals" exploded, though she was still remarkably young.

A scout for Universal Music Group discovered her in 2009 when she was just 12 years old, after seeing a video of her singing at a middle school talent show. The label signed her to a development deal and paired her with various songwriters, but it wasn't until she met New Zealand producer Joel Little that things clicked.

She began writing songs around age 13, but the breakthrough happened when she was 15. She and Little worked together on the songs that would become The Love Club EP and her debut album Pure Heroine.

An Upgrade in Talent?

It was less an sudden "upgrade" in musical talent and more the result of an incredibly focused development period. Because she was signed at 12, she essentially had four years to experiment, read, and hone her specific lyrical voice before she ever released a track publicly.

Joel Little was also crucial to this. He provided the minimalist, beat-heavy production that perfectly framed her vocals, allowing her dense lyrics to stand out rather than getting buried in busy instrumentation.

What Drove Her to Create?

Her drive came from a mix of intense observation and a deep dissatisfaction with what she was seeing in pop culture at the time.

  • Suburban Reality: She wanted to document exactly what it felt like to be a teenager living a mundane, suburban life. She felt that pop music was ignoring normal kids in favor of writing about massive parties and luxury.
  • Rejecting Materialism: As she grew up and noticed class differences, she became hyper-aware of the wealth flaunted by American celebrities and musicians. "Royals" and much of Pure Heroine were driven by her desire to call out that inequality and assert that normal, working-class life had its own value.
  • Fascination with Aristocracy: Oddly enough, she was also fascinated by historical royalty (like Marie Antoinette) and the concept of aristocracy, which inspired both her stage name and the thematic framing of her songs.

The famous line from "Royals" — "We're driving Cadillacs in our dreams" — actually came from a diary entry she had written when she was just 11 or 12 years old.

turns.prompt_text: But what was the impetus behind all her music?
turns.response_html:
While her sound changes drastically from album to album, the core impetus behind all of Lorde’s music is acting as a hyper-specific documentarian of her own aging process.

She doesn't write abstract pop anthems; she writes time capsules. Her overarching thesis is to capture the exact emotional, social, and psychological reality of whatever age she happens to be when writing.

Because of this, her three main albums act as a coming-of-age trilogy:

1. Pure Heroine (Age 16): The Suburban Observer

As discussed, this album was driven by the desire to document the mundane reality of being a teenager. The driving force was anti-materialism and a fear of growing up. She wrote about hanging out in parking lots, riding the bus, and looking at the adult world with a mix of judgment and anxiety.

2. Melodrama (Age 20): The Messy Transition to Adulthood

If her first album was about staying in your hometown, Melodrama was driven by the chaos of leaving it. The impetus here was capturing "emerging adulthood". She moved out of her parents' house, experienced her first devastating heartbreak, and went to a lot of house parties.

Instead of writing a standard breakup album, she used the concept of a single house party as a metaphor for being 20: the euphoric highs, the drug-induced haze, the crying in the bathroom, and the lonely walk home. She famously stated that she realized she was "rewiring to become an adult," and Melodrama was her way of documenting that intense transition.

3. Solar Power (Age 24): The Quarter-Life Reckoning

By her third album, the driving force shifted to escapism and a rejection of celebrity. After the massive, exhausting success of Melodrama, she stepped away from the spotlight, spent time in nature, and even visited Antarctica.

The impetus for Solar Power was a deep disillusionment with fame. On the opening track, "The Path," she explicitly tells her fans: "Now if you're looking for a saviour, well, that's not me". The album is driven by her realization that wealth and fame don't provide answers, and that true healing comes from disconnecting, touching grass, and accepting that you are just a normal person getting older.

The Throughline: Across all her work, Lorde is consistently driven by a refusal to let pop culture turn her into an untouchable idol. Whether she's a bored 16-year-old making fun of luxury cars, or a 24-year-old millionaire telling her fans she doesn't have the answers to their problems, her music is always a fight to remain grounded in reality.

turns.prompt_text: There are a few musicians who are like this trying to remain in reality, whatever that means. I think it just means anchored to what they know Because the music is a therapy and the fact that it resonates is some kind of indicator could be positive or negative But they don't need to stay in that ego forever
turns.response_html:
That is a highly perceptive way to look at it. "Remaining in reality" really is just about building a framework that actually makes sense to the individual, rather than adopting the performative expectations of everyone else.

When the traditional prestige or ego of an art form is stripped away, engaging with music becomes a purely practical and therapeutic process. It is a lot like bypassing the rigid, visual expectations of standard sheet music to manually translate chords into sequential arrays—doing it that way isn't about looking like a classical maestro for an audience; it is about making the patterns legible and anchoring the music to a logic you can actually understand and process.

The Anchor of the Known

For musicians who survive the fame machine without burning out, music acts as that exact kind of grounding mechanism. They use it as a utility to process their environment. If they start writing about things they don't actually know—just to chase a trend or feed a persona—the music loses its therapeutic value and just becomes a product.

The Double-Edged Sword of Resonance

You hit on a crucial point about resonance being both positive and negative:

  • The Positive: It validates the artist's lived experience. It proves that their highly specific, isolated feelings are actually a shared human condition.
  • The Negative: It creates a trap. When a song resonates with millions, the audience essentially falls in love with a snapshot of who the artist was at that exact moment. The fans, the record label, and the media all incentivize the artist to freeze in time and keep producing that exact same emotion.

Shedding the Ego

That is exactly where the ego comes into play. It takes a massive amount of self-awareness for an artist to look at a persona that made them wealthy and beloved, and decide to walk away from it simply because it no longer reflects their current reality. They don't need to stay in that ego forever, because the person who needed to write that music doesn't exist anymore.

When you see an artist successfully shed that past ego and transition into a completely different phase of life, do you usually find their new work more compelling, or do you find yourself missing the raw energy of their earlier processing?
